claim: Flows generated by ensembles of flagella are crucial to development, motility and sensing.
source: Flows generated by ensembles of flagella are crucial to development, motility and sensing, but the mechanisms behind this striking coordination remain unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of flagellar flows, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Two micropipette-held somatic cells of Volvox carteri with distinct intrinsic beating frequencies were studied by high-speed imaging as a function of their separation and orientation.
source: We present novel experiments in which two micropipette-held somatic cells of Volvox carteri, with distinct intrinsic beating frequencies, are studied by high-speed imaging as a function of their separation and orientation.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and methodology used in the study.

claim: The interflagellar coupling is constrained by lack of connections between cells to be hydrodynamical.
source: Analysis of time series shows that the interflagellar coupling, constrained by lack of connections between cells to be hydrodynamical, exhibits a spatial dependence consistent with theory.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design where cells are physically separated, precluding non-hydrodynamic coupling.

claim: The interflagellar coupling exhibits a spatial dependence consistent with theory.
source: Analysis of time series shows that the interflagellar coupling, constrained by lack of connections between cells to be hydrodynamical, exhibits a spatial dependence consistent with theory.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements compared with theoretical predictions.

claim: At close spacings, hydrodynamic coupling produces robust synchrony for thousands of beats.
source: At close spacings it produces robust synchrony for thousands of beats, while at increasing separations synchrony is degraded by stochastic processes.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: At increasing separations, synchrony is degraded by stochastic processes.
source: At close spacings it produces robust synchrony for thousands of beats, while at increasing separations synchrony is degraded by stochastic processes.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and analyzed through the stochastic model.

claim: Manipulation of the relative flagellar orientation reveals in-phase and antiphase states.
source: Manipulation of the relative flagellar orientation reveals in-phase and antiphase states, consistent with dynamical theories.
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments where pipettes were rotated to change flagellar orientation.

claim: The observed in-phase and antiphase states are consistent with dynamical theories.
source: Manipulation of the relative flagellar orientation reveals in-phase and antiphase states, consistent with dynamical theories.
evidence: Experimental observations are compared with theoretical predictions.

claim: Flagellar tracking with exquisite precision reveals waveform changes that result from hydrodynamic coupling.
source: Flagellar tracking with exquisite precision reveals waveform changes that result from hydrodynamic coupling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through dynamic tracking experiments showing waveform changes at different separations.

claim: Flagella coupled solely through a fluid can achieve robust synchrony despite differences in their intrinsic properties.
source: This study proves unequivocally that flagella coupled solely through a fluid can achieve robust synchrony despite differences in their intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii executes diffusive 'run-and-turn' locomotion through stochastic switching between synchronized and unsynchronized swimming gaits.
source: For example, the unicellular biflagellate alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii executes diffusive 'run-and-turn' locomotion (Goldstein et al., 2009; Polin et al., 2009) through stochastic switching between synchronized and unsynchronized swimming gaits—a process which could enhance searching efficiency and assist in the avoidance of predators (Stocker and Durham, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ensembles of cilia and flagella generate flows that transport mucus and expel pathogens.
source: Ensembles of cilia and flagella exhibit stunning temporal coordination, generating flows that transport mucus and expel pathogens (Button et al., 2012), establish the left-right asymmetry in developing mammalian embryos (Nonaka et al., 2002), and transport ova in human fallopian tubes (Lyons et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Button et al., 2012.

claim: Ensembles of cilia and flagella establish the left-right asymmetry in developing mammalian embryos.
source: Ensembles of cilia and flagella exhibit stunning temporal coordination, generating flows that transport mucus and expel pathogens (Button et al., 2012), establish the left-right asymmetry in developing mammalian embryos (Nonaka et al., 2002), and transport ova in human fallopian tubes (Lyons et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nonaka et al., 2002.

claim: Ensembles of cilia and flagella transport ova in human fallopian tubes.
source: Ensembles of cilia and flagella exhibit stunning temporal coordination, generating flows that transport mucus and expel pathogens (Button et al., 2012), establish the left-right asymmetry in developing mammalian embryos (Nonaka et al., 2002), and transport ova in human fallopian tubes (Lyons et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lyons et al., 2006.

claim: Rothschild qualitatively observed that the flagella of bull spermatozoa tend to synchronize when they swim close to one another, coupled only through the fluid surrounding them.
source: One of the earliest experimental results was Rothschild's qualitative observation (Rothschild, 1949) that the flagella of bull spermatozoa tend to synchronize when they swim close to one another, coupled only through the fluid surrounding them.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rothschild, 1949.

claim: Self-organised vortex arrays of swimming sea urchin spermatozoa near surfaces provide evidence for synchrony mediated purely by hydrodynamic coupling.
source: Much more recent observations of self-organised vortex arrays of swimming sea urchin spermatazoa near surfaces (Riedel et al., 2005) provide further evidence for synchrony mediated purely by hydrodynamic coupling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riedel et al., 2005.

claim: Taylor developed a mathematical model in which two laterally infinite, inextensible sheets with prescribed sinusoidal travelling waves of transverse deformation interact through a viscous fluid.
source: Motivated by Rothschild's observation, Taylor (Taylor, 1951) developed a mathematical model in which two laterally infinite, inextensible sheets with prescribed sinusoidal travelling waves of transverse deformation interact with each other through a viscous fluid.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taylor, 1951.

claim: Taylor found that the rate of viscous dissipation is minimised when the two sheets are in phase.
source: He found that the rate of viscous dissipation is minimised when the two sheets are in phase.
evidence: This is a result from Taylor's theoretical work.

claim: Hydrodynamically coupled filaments or chains with various internal driving forces exhibit a general tendency towards synchrony.
source: Hydrodynamically coupled filaments or chains with various internal driving forces exhibit a general tendency towards synchrony (Machin, 1963; Gueron et al., 1997; Guirao and Joanny, 2007; Yang et al., 2008; Elgeti and Gompper, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Minimal models of coupled oscillators in viscous fluids offer great insight into the emergence of metachronal coordination.
source: At the same time, minimal models of coupled oscillators in viscous fluids (Vilfan and Jülicher, 2006; Niedermayer et al., 2008; Uchida and Golestanian, 2011, 2012; Brumley et al., 2012) offer great insight into the emergence of metachronal coordination.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies.

claim: Experimentally-derived coupling strengths between micropipette-held Chlamydomonas flagella are consistent with predictions based on direct hydrodynamic coupling.
source: Although experimentally-derived coupling strengths between micropipette-held Chlamydomonas flagella are consistent with predictions based on direct hydrodynamic coupling (Goldstein et al., 2011), it has been proposed (Friedrich and Jülicher, 2012; Geyer et al., 2013) instead that this coupling is too weak to overcome noise, and that residual motion of elastically-clamped cells could play a role in synchronization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldstein et al., 2011.

claim: It has been proposed that hydrodynamic coupling is too weak to overcome noise and that residual motion of elastically-clamped cells could play a role in synchronization.
source: Although experimentally-derived coupling strengths between micropipette-held Chlamydomonas flagella are consistent with predictions based on direct hydrodynamic coupling (Goldstein et al., 2011), it has been proposed (Friedrich and Jülicher, 2012; Geyer et al., 2013) instead that this coupling is too weak to overcome noise, and that residual motion of elastically-clamped cells could play a role in synchronization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedrich and Jülicher, 2012 and Geyer et al., 2013.

claim: The observation of antiphase synchronization in a non-phototactic mutant of Chlamydomonas points to the possible role of internal mechanical coupling between flagella.
source: The recent observation (Leptos et al., 2013) of antiphase synchronization in a non-phototactic mutant of Chlamydomonas points as well to the possible role of internal mechanical coupling between flagella.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leptos et al., 2013.

claim: Each somatic cell of Volvox carteri possesses two flagella which beat in perfect synchrony.
source: Each somatic cell possesses two flagella which beat in perfect synchrony, facilitating their treatment as a single entity, henceforth referred to as the flagellum.
evidence: This is an observation about the biological system used in the experiments.

claim: Closely-separated pairs of cells can exhibit robust phase-locking for thousands of beats at a time, despite a discrepancy in their intrinsic frequencies of as much as 10%.
source: We found that closely-separated pairs of cells can exhibit robust phase-locking for thousands of beats at a time, despite a discrepancy in their intrinsic frequencies of as much as 10%.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: Both in-phase and antiphase configurations were observed, depending on the alignment of the directions of flagellar propulsion.
source: Both in-phase and antiphase configurations were observed, depending on the alignment of the directions of flagellar propulsion.
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments where flagellar orientation was manipulated.

claim: With increasing interflagellar spacing, a marked change in the beating waveform was observed for each flagellum.
source: Furthermore, with increasing interflagellar spacing we observed for each flagellum a marked change in the beating waveform, a key finding that lends support to models of synchronization that rely on waveform compliance to achieve phase-locking.
evidence: This is directly observed through flagellar tracking experiments.

claim: The time-averaged flow around a flagellum can be approximated by the flow from a point force at a suitable average location.
source: In the simplest case, often used in models of synchronization (Vilfan and Jülicher, 2006; Niedermayer et al., 2008; Uchida and Golestanian, 2011), that would be just a single sphere tracing out a closed orbit in space under the action of internal driving forces. The time-averaged flow around the flagellum would then be approximated by the flow from a point force at a suitable average location.
evidence: This is a theoretical approximation commonly used in modeling.

claim: The time-averaged flow field of freely swimming Chlamydomonas cells is consistent with a three-Stokeslet model.
source: A recent study (Drescher et al., 2010) of freely swimming Chlamydomonas cells has shown that the time-averaged flow field is consistent in its magnitude and topology with a three-Stokeslet model (one for each flagellum and one for the cell body).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drescher et al., 2010.

claim: For distances larger than 20 μm from the flagellar tip, both upstream and downstream components of the flow obey a Stokeslet decay (u ∼ 1/r).
source: Examining the time-averaged velocity field (Figure 2B, obtained by averaging data from four cells), we see that for distances larger than 20 μm from the flagellar tip, both upstream (red) and downstream (blue) components of the flow obey a Stokeslet decay (u ∼ 1/r) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through PIV measurements and analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The orientation of the point force does not coincide with its direction of motion.
source: Importantly, the orientation of the point force does not coincide with its direction of motion, a feature to be expected given the anisotropic drag on the flagellum.
evidence: This is observed in the Stokeslet fitting analysis and explained by the physics of anisotropic drag.

claim: The amplitude of the fitted Stokeslet force is approximated by F(t)/8πμ=A0(1+A1sin(2πt/T)) with A0 ≃ 1076 μm²/s and A1 ≃ 0.56.
source: The amplitude of this force exhibits very strong periodic variations, and is approximated by F(t)/8πμ=A0(1+A1sin(2πt/T)) with A0 ≃ 1076 μm2/s and A1 ≃ 0.56.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental flow field data to a Stokeslet model.

claim: Resistive force theory considers the anisotropic drag experienced by a long rod-like flagellum moving through a viscous fluid.
source: First proposed by Gray and Hancock (1955), RFT considers the anisotropic drag experienced by a long rod-like flagellum moving through a viscous fluid, and assumes that each unit segment of the flagellum experiences a local drag that is proportional to its local instantaneous velocity.
evidence: This is a description of resistive force theory, supported by citation to Gray and Hancock, 1955.

claim: The force density along the flagellum is approximated by f=C⊥u⊥+C‖u‖.
source: The force density f along the flagellum is approximated by(1)f=C⊥u⊥+C‖u‖,which is readily computable from experimental data, where the constants of proportionality, C⊥ and C‖, are the normal and tangential resistance coefficients respectively.
evidence: This is the mathematical formulation of resistive force theory.

claim: The amplitude of the force calculated using RFT is similar to the value calculated using Stokeslet fitting.
source: It is encouraging to see that the amplitude of this force is similar to the value calculated earlier using Stokeslet fitting, though it should be noted that these results correspond to two different cells.
evidence: This is a comparison of results from two different analytical methods applied to experimental data.

claim: For L≳2, hydrodynamic coupling is negligible and Δ(t) drifts approximately linearly with time depending on δω/ω.
source: Calling L = d/l the cell–cell separation normalised by the average flagellar length l of each pair, Figure 1C shows that for L≳2 hydrodynamic coupling is negligible and Δ(t) drifts approximately linearly with time depending on δω/ω (8.2% here).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: For intermediate values of L, the flagella exhibit short periods of synchrony interrupted by brief phase slips.
source: For intermediate values of L, the flagella exhibit short periods of synchrony interrupted by brief phase slips.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data.

claim: When cells are brought closer to each other, they phase-lock for the entire duration of the experiment.
source: However, when the same cells are brought closer to each other, they phase-lock for the entire duration of the experiment.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: Cells aligned so that their power strokes point in the same direction exhibit in-phase synchrony (Δ0 ≃ 0), indicating a coupling strength ϵ>0.
source: Cells aligned so that their power strokes point in the same direction (as in many ciliates) exhibit in-phase (IP) synchrony (Δ0 ≃ 0), indicating a coupling strength ϵ>0.
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments with specific flagellar orientations.

claim: Rotation of pipette P1 by 180° so that the power strokes are opposed changes the sign of the coupling strength and gives rise to antiphase synchronization (Δ0 ≃ 1/2).
source: Rotation of pipette P1 (Figure 1B) by 180∘ so that the power strokes are opposed (as in the Chlamydomonas breaststroke) changes the sign of the coupling strength and gives rise to antiphase (AP) synchronization (Δ0 ≃ 1/2), in agreement with theory (Leptos et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly observed in experiments and compared with theoretical predictions.

claim: The dependence of coupling strength on interflagellar spacing is |κ|∝L⁻¹.
source: The dependence on the interflagellar spacing |κ|∝L−1 is consistent with the intrinsic flagellar flow field presented in Figure 2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fitting experimental data and comparing with flow field measurements.

claim: For in-phase configuration, the coupling strength fit yields kIP = 0.016.
source: For both the in-phase and antiphase configurations, we fit |κ|=k×L−1 finding kIP = 0.016 and kAP = 0.014 respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data.

claim: For antiphase configuration, the coupling strength fit yields kAP = 0.014.
source: For both the in-phase and antiphase configurations, we fit |κ|=k×L−1 finding kIP = 0.016 and kAP = 0.014 respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting experimental data.

claim: At a given L, in-phase pairs exhibit on average a marginally stronger coupling than antiphase ones.
source: At a given L, IP pairs exhibit on average a marginally stronger coupling than AP ones, possibly due to the fact that flagella in IP are on average closer together than in AP.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and explained by geometric considerations.

claim: The average values of model parameters are 〈Teff/ω̄〉=0.005±0.003 and 〈δν/ω̄〉=0.058±0.033, with 〈ω̄〉=33.0 Hz.
source: The average values of the other model parameters are 〈Teff/ω¯〉=0.005±0.003 and 〈δν/ω¯〉=0.058±0.033, with 〈ω¯〉=33.0 Hz.
evidence: These are parameters extracted from fitting the stochastic model to experimental data.

claim: The effective internal noise estimated directly from the distribution of beating periods of separated cells is 〈Teff/ω̄〉=0.002.
source: As a cross-check, we can estimate directly the effective internal noise from the distribution of beating periods of separated cells, and find 〈Teff/ω¯〉=0.002, consistent with the value above.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements of beating period variability.

claim: Noise plays an important role in determining the observed location of the bifurcation point.
source: It is evident that noise plays an important role in determining the observed location of the bifurcation point.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing deterministic and stochastic model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Models of coupled flagella involving hydrodynamically coupled semiflexible filaments show a tendency towards metachronal coordination.
source: Indeed, models of coupled flagella involving hydrodynamically coupled semiflexible filaments (Gueron et al., 1997; Guirao and Joanny, 2007; Elgeti and Gompper, 2013; Yang et al., 2008) show a tendency towards metachronal coordination, though the precise role that flexibility plays in facilitating synchrony is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies.

claim: Minimal models in which spheres are driven along flexible trajectories reveal that deformation-induced changes in the phase speed can facilitate synchrony.
source: Minimal models in which spheres are driven along flexible trajectories (Brumley et al., 2012; Niedermayer et al., 2008) reveal that deformation-induced changes in the phase speed can facilitate synchrony.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical modeling studies.

claim: Functional variations in the intrinsic flagellar driving forces could lead to synchrony even for fixed beating patterns.
source: However, functional variations in the intrinsic flagellar driving forces could lead to synchrony even for fixed beating patterns (Uchida and Golestanian, 2011, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: The most significant waveform difference is observed in the xc component (distal part of the flagellum).
source: In particular, the most significant difference is observed in the xc component (distal part of the flagellum).
evidence: This is observed through detailed flagellar tracking analysis.

claim: The interaction between flagella is mutual, with both flagella showing waveform changes.
source: Similar results are found for the other cell, indicating that the interaction is mutual.
evidence: This is observed by analyzing both flagella in the experiments.

claim: Each flagellum can directly alter the beating profile of its neighbour simply through hydrodynamic interactions.
source: Taken together, the results in Figure 6 demonstrate that accompanying the robust hydrodynamic phase-locking is a change in the flagellar waveform. For the first time, we have shown by systematically varying the cell–cell spacing that each flagellum can directly alter the beating profile of its neighbour simply through hydrodynamic interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic experiments varying cell-cell spacing and tracking waveform changes.

claim: Cell body rocking of freely swimming Chlamydomonas can induce synchrony.
source: Theoretical studies and experiments suggest that cell body rocking of freely swimming Chlamydomonas can induce synchrony (Friedrich and Jülicher, 2012; Geyer et al., 2013), and experimental investigations of such cells hint that hydrodynamic interactions between the flagella and cell body could be important for locomotion (Kurtuldu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and experimental studies.

claim: The synchronization properties of immobilised Chlamydomonas cells are generally consistent with models in which the flagella interact purely hydrodynamically.
source: At the same time, the synchronization properties of immobilised Chlamydomonas cells are generally consistent with models in which the flagella interact purely hydrodynamically (Goldstein et al., 2009, 2011; Polin et al., 2009), although the observed antiphase synchronization of the ptx1 mutant has been suggested (Leptos et al., 2013) to implicate intracellular coupling such as through elastic filaments at the basal bodies.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Intracellular calcium fluctuations in Chlamydomonas are known to affect the flagellar dynamics.
source: In addition, intracellular calcium fluctuations in Chlamydomonas are known to affect the flagellar dynamics (Yoshimura et al., 2003; Leptos et al., 2013), so these studies cannot exclude the possibility that flagellar synchrony is regulated primarily by chemical or other non-mechanical means.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Machemer showed that membrane voltage affects the metachronal wave direction in Paramecium.
source: Indeed, Machemer showed that membrane voltage affects the metachronal wave direction in Paramecium (Machemer, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Machemer, 1972.

claim: The fact that the coupling strength for in-phase and antiphase pairs is almost identical despite the pronounced difference between the associated flows rules out coupling via chemical means.
source: The fact that the coupling strength for IP and AP pairs is almost identical despite the pronounced difference between the associated flows rules out coupling via chemical means.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and comparison of coupling strengths.

claim: The estimated rotational spring constant is k > 3 × 10⁴ pN·μm, which is sufficiently large to suggest that rocking does not play a significant role in the synchronization.
source: We have performed experiments of exactly this type, in which we measured the rocking motion of a deflagellated cell placed in the flow field of a cell with a beating flagellum (Video 2), and found α* ≤ 0.01 (about 0.5°). This strongly suggests k > 3 × 104 pN·μm, which, by the calculations of Geyer et al. (2013), is sufficiently large to suggest that rocking does not play a significant role in the synchronization observed in the present experiments.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental measurements of cell rocking and compared with theoretical predictions.

claim: Physical separation of the cells precludes any form of chemical or direct mechanical coupling, leaving hydrodynamic interactions as the only mechanism through which synchronization can occur.
source: The experimental study presented in this article reveals unambiguously the importance of hydrodynamics in achieving flagellar synchronization. Physical separation of the cells precludes any form of chemical or direct mechanical coupling, leaving hydrodynamic interactions as the only mechanism through which synchronization can occur.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the experimental design.

claim: The process of phase-locking is extremely robust, with cells sufficiently close to one another exhibiting uninterrupted synchrony for thousands of consecutive beats.
source: The process of phase-locking is extremely robust, with cells sufficiently close to one another exhibiting uninterrupted synchrony for thousands of consecutive beats.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: The extracted interflagellar coupling strength is consistent with hydrodynamic predictions and the measured flow fields generated by individual flagella.
source: The extracted interflagellar coupling strength is consistent with hydrodynamic predictions and the measured flow fields generated by individual flagella.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing extracted coupling strengths with theoretical predictions and flow field measurements.

claim: Hydrodynamic phase-locking was also observed in experiments using a uniflagellar mutant of Chlamydomonas.
source: Additional experiments were undertaken using a uniflagellar mutant of the unicellular alga Chlamydomonas. Although its flagellum is shorter and its waveform is different to that of Volvox, we also observed hydrodynamic phase-locking in these experiments.
evidence: This is directly observed in additional experiments with a different organism.

claim: The results of the present study are expected to generalise to other systems due to the ubiquity and uniformity in the structure and function of flagella in various eukaryotic species.
source: Owing to the ubiquity and uniformity in the structure and function of flagella in various eukaryotic species, the results of the present study are expected to generalise to other systems, and may be of significant value for a wide range of theoretical models.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the findings based on biological knowledge.

claim: Volvox carteri f. nagariensis (strain EVE) were grown axenically in Standard Volvox Medium with sterile air bubbling in a growth chamber set to a cycle of 16 hr light at 28°C and 8 hr dark at 26°C.
source: Volvox carteri f. nagariensis (strain EVE) were grown axenically in Standard Volvox Medium (SVM) (Kirk and Kirk, 1983) with sterile air bubbling, in a growth chamber (Binder, Germany) set to a cycle of 16 hr light (100 μEm−2s−1, Fluora, OSRAM) at 28∘C and 8 hr dark at 26∘C.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for cell culture.

claim: Videos were recorded with a high-speed video camera at 1000 fps under bright field illumination.
source: For each experiment, we recorded videos with a high-speed video camera (Fastcam SA3, Photron, USA) at 1000 fps under bright field illumination.
evidence: This describes the experimental imaging methodology.

claim: The time-dependent velocity field was reconstructed using particle image velocimetry.
source: The time-dependent velocity field was reconstructed using an open source particle image velocimetry (Raffel et al., 2007) toolbox for MATLAB (MatPIV).
evidence: This describes the method used for flow field analysis.

claim: The second pipette affects the flow, but mostly in the region between the two pipettes.
source: It is clear that the second pipette affects the flow, but mostly in the region between the two pipettes.
evidence: This is observed in control experiments examining the effect of pipette proximity.

claim: For a cell held from the side, the flow in the region upstream of the cell is only minimally affected, with an average relative change below 8%.
source: Let us consider the region upstream of the cell (above the cell in Figure 8). For a cell held from the side, this is the region where the other cell will be. Here the flow is only minimally affected, with an average relative change between Figure 8D,A below 8%.
evidence: This is measured in control experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Within the minimal model with variable forcing, the two oscillators synchronize through a coupling between hydrodynamic stresses and orbit compliance with no noticeable effect from force modulation.
source: These results show clearly that within the boundary of the model we are considering, the two oscillators synchronize through a coupling between hydrodynamic stresses and orbit compliance (Niedermayer et al., 2008) with no noticeable effect from force modulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations of the minimal model.
